quiz: An inner join only returns matched pairs. Count how many orders actually find a customer.
A left join keeps every matched row plus one NULL-filled row for each left row with no match.
A full outer join keeps matches plus unmatched rows from both sides.
Any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, and joins keep only pairs whose condition is TRUE.
Think about what happens to NULL-filled rows when WHERE tests a column from the optional table.
Put the filter where it only limits which rows can match, not where it removes rows after the join.
If the subquery list contains a NULL, x NOT IN that list can never be TRUE.
Pick the form that only checks whether a match exists and never repeats the outer row.
A cross join pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, so multiply.
Two independent one-to-many branches multiply each other for the same order.
DISTINCT removes repeated values, not repeated rows, so real equal payments would be lost.
Someone with no manager has no matching row, and a left join fills the missing side with NULL.
A later inner join compares against the NULL-filled columns from the earlier left join.
It matches on columns automatically, based on the column names the two tables share.
Inner joins keep only TRUE pairs, so ON and WHERE only differ for outer joins.
interview: Use a simple everyday picture for each join type: matches only, all of left, all of right, and all of both with blanks for missing.
Explain that ON applies while matching and WHERE after, why they are the same for inner joins, and how WHERE can turn a left join into an inner one.
Write a self join of employees to their managers and discuss NULL managers, ties, NULL salaries, and why inner join fits.
Explain how NOT IN expands to ANDed comparisons where a NULL makes it never TRUE, and alternatives like NOT EXISTS or a left join anti-join.
Define a semi-join and explain why EXISTS can stop at the first match while JOIN plus DISTINCT multiplies then removes rows.
Name the fan-out or chasm trap, how to check row grain and key uniqueness, and fix it by pre-aggregating payments per order.
Use a full outer join and keep rows where either key is NULL, labelled with CASE, plus a workaround for engines without full joins.
Describe the Cartesian product, its symptoms like huge counts and inflated totals, and how to estimate and check row counts.
Compare nested loop, hash and merge joins: how each works, cost, which conditions they support, and when each is chosen.
Call it relational division and show double NOT EXISTS or a counting approach with GROUP BY and HAVING.
Give deliberate uses: generating combinations, a scaffold for zero-filled reports, and attaching a single-row value to every row.
Look for null-rejecting filters or later inner joins on the optional table, and build the query step by step checking row counts.
Compare ON and USING in conditions and output columns, and explain how NATURAL JOIN silently joins on every shared column name.
Cover foreign keys with matching types, indexing child-side foreign key columns, composite and covering indexes, and checking plans.
